## Definition

A **directional hypothesis** (one-tailed) specifies not only that there will be a difference or relationship, but also the direction of that effect.

## Key Characteristics

| Feature | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| Specifies direction | States which group will be higher/lower |
| One-tailed test | Critical region in one tail only |
| More specific | Makes a precise prediction |
| More power | Easier to detect effect in predicted direction |

## Examples

| Non-directional | Directional |
|-----------------|-------------|
| "There will be a difference..." | "Group A will score **higher** than..." |
| "...will affect..." | "...will **increase**..." |
| "...will be related to..." | "...will be **positively** related to..." |

## When to Use Directional Hypotheses

Use when:

- Strong theoretical basis for direction
- Previous research consistently shows direction
- Only one direction makes logical sense
- Only interested in effect in one direction

## One-Tailed vs. Two-Tailed Tests

```
Two-tailed (non-directional):
        ┌──2.5%──┐         ┌──2.5%──┐
        │░░░░░░░░│         │░░░░░░░░│
────────┴────────┴─────────┴────────┴────────
       -1.96     0        +1.96

One-tailed (directional, predicting higher):
                           ┌───5%───┐
                           │░░░░░░░░│
───────────────────────────┴────────┴────────
                  0       +1.65

Critical value lower → easier to reach significance
```

## Advantages and Disadvantages

| Advantages | Disadvantages |
|------------|---------------|
| More statistical power | Cannot detect opposite effects |
| Lower critical value | Must justify direction a priori |
| Matches specific predictions | Can seem like p-hacking if chosen after data |

## Important Rule

You must choose directional or non-directional **before** collecting data. Choosing after seeing the data is inappropriate and inflates Type I error.

## DataLab Connection

For **Reflex Test**, a directional hypothesis is appropriate: "Reaction times will be significantly **slower** in the choice condition than in the simple condition" (based on well-established Hick's Law).
